name: Wi-Fi Networks
title: T1669 Wi-Fi Networks: what it is
text:
T1669 Wi-Fi Networks. Tactic: Initial Access. Platforms: Linux, Network Devices, Windows, macOS.
Adversaries may gain initial access to target systems by connecting to wireless networks. They may accomplish this by exploiting open Wi-Fi networks used by target devices or by accessing secured Wi-Fi networks — requiring Valid Accounts — belonging to a target organization. Establishing a connection to a Wi-Fi access point requires a certain level of proximity to both discover and maintain a stable network connection.
Adversaries may establish a wireless connection through various methods, such as by physically positioning themselves near a Wi-Fi network to conduct close access operations. To bypass the need for physical proximity, adversaries may attempt to remotely compromise nearby third-party systems that have both wired and wireless network connections available (i.e., dual-homed systems). These third-party compromised devices can then serve as a bridge to connect to a target’s Wi-Fi network.
Once an initial wireless connection is achieved, adversaries may leverage this access for follow-on activities in the victim network or further targeting of specific devices on the network. Adversaries may perform Network Sniffing or Adversary-in-the-Middle activities for Credential Access or Discovery.

name: Wi-Fi Networks
title: T1669 Wi-Fi Networks: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1669 Wi-Fi Networks.
Detection strategy: Detection Strategy for Wi-Fi Networks.
Windows: Detects anomalous wireless connections such as unexpected SSID associations, failed or repeated authentication attempts, and connections outside of known geofenced networks. Defenders should monitor wireless connection logs and event codes for network discovery, authentication, and association events. Log sources: WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WLAN-AutoConfig, WinEventLog:Security.
Linux: Detects unauthorized wireless associations by monitoring wpa_supplicant logs, NetworkManager events, and system calls related to interface state changes. Anomalies include repeated association failures, new SSIDs outside baselined values, and rogue AP connections. Log sources: linux:syslog, auditd:SYSCALL.
macOS: Detects unauthorized Wi-Fi associations and SSID scanning activity using unified logs and airport command telemetry. Anomalies include rapid SSID switching, connections to unapproved SSIDs, or repeated authentication failures. Log sources: macos:unifiedlog, macos:osquery.
Network Devices: Detects rogue or suspicious wireless access attempts by monitoring firewall, WIDS/WIPS, and controller logs. Focus is on firewall rule changes, rogue AP detection, and anomalous MAC addresses connecting to access points. Log sources: NSM:Firewall, WIDS:AssociationLogs.

name: Wi-Fi Networks
title: T1669 Wi-Fi Networks: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1669 Wi-Fi Networks.
M1032 Multi-factor Authentication: Harden access requirements for Wi-Fi networks through using two or more pieces of evidence to authenticate, such as a username and password in addition to a token from a physical smart card or token generator.
M1030 Network Segmentation: Network segmentation can be used to isolate infrastructure components that do not require broad network access. Separate networking environments for Wi-Fi and Ethernet-wired networks, particularly where Ethernet-based networks allow for access to sensitive resources.
M1041 Encrypt Sensitive Information: Ensure that all wired and/or wireless traffic is encrypted appropriately. Use best practices for authentication protocols, such as Kerberos, and ensure that web traffic that may contain credentials is protected by SSL/TLS.

name: Wi-Fi Networks
title: T1669 Wi-Fi Networks: threat groups that use it
text: Threat groups known to use T1669 Wi-Fi Networks (1): APT28.

name: Exploitation for Stealth
title: T1211 Exploitation for Stealth: what it is
text:
T1211 Exploitation for Stealth. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: Linux, Windows, macOS, SaaS, IaaS.
Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities to evade detection by hiding activity, suppressing logging, or operating within trusted or unmonitored components.
Adversaries may exploit a system or application vulnerability to avoid detection while maintaining access within an environment. Exploitation occurs when an adversary leverages a programming flaw to execute code in a manner that minimizes visibility or blends in with legitimate activity.
Rather than directly disabling defenses, adversaries may use exploitation to circumvent monitoring and logging mechanisms. This can include abusing vulnerabilities in logging pipelines, security tools, or cloud infrastructure to evade audit trails, suppress alerts, or operate without generating telemetry.
Adversaries may identify these opportunities through prior reconnaissance or by performing discovery of security controls after initial access. In some cases, vulnerabilities in SaaS or public cloud environments may be exploited to evade logging, obscure activity, or deploy infrastructure that remains hidden from standard monitoring tools.

name: Exploitation for Stealth
title: T1211 Exploitation for Stealth: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1211 Exploitation for Stealth.
Detection strategy: Detection Strategy for Exploitation for Stealth.
Windows: Detects exploitation attempts targeting defensive security software or OS services. Defender observation includes abnormal process behavior (e.g., AV or EDR crashing unexpectedly), unsigned/untrusted modules loaded into defensive processes, or privilege escalation from security agent services. Multi-event correlation ties exploitation attempts to subsequent evasive behavior like service termination or missing logs. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security, WinEventLog:Sysmon.
Linux: Detects kernel- or user-space exploitation attempts targeting auditd, AV daemons, or security monitoring agents. Defender observation includes unexpected segfaults, privilege escalation attempts from low-privileged processes, or modifications to security binaries. Correlates exploitation attempts with subsequent gaps in logging or terminated processes. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL, linux:syslog.
macOS: Detects exploitation of macOS security and integrity services, such as Gatekeeper, XProtect, or EDR agents. Defender observations include unsigned processes attempting privileged operations, abnormal termination of security daemons, or modification of system integrity logs. Log sources: macos:unifiedlog, macos:osquery.
IaaS: Detects exploitation of IaaS cloud security boundaries to evade defense controls. Defender perspective includes anomalous API calls that bypass audit logging, disable monitoring, or manipulate guardrails (e.g., CloudTrail tampering). Correlation highlights when exploitation attempts precede sudden absence of expected telemetry. Log sources: AWS:CloudTrail.

name: Exploitation for Stealth
title: T1211 Exploitation for Stealth: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1211 Exploitation for Stealth.
SaaS: Detects adversary abuse of SaaS platform vulnerabilities to bypass logging, monitoring, or consent boundaries. Defender perspective focuses on abnormal application integration events, missing audit logs, or API calls from unauthorized service principals that align with exploitation attempts. Log sources: m365:unified.

name: Exploitation for Stealth
title: T1211 Exploitation for Stealth: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1211 Exploitation for Stealth.
M1050 Exploit Protection: Security applications that look for behavior used during exploitation such as Windows Defender Exploit Guard (WDEG) and the Enhanced Mitigation Experience Toolkit (EMET) can be used to mitigate some exploitation behavior. Control flow integrity checking is another way to potentially identify and stop a software exploit from occurring. Many of these protections depend on the architecture and target application binary for compatibility and may not work for software targeted for defense evasion.
M1051 Update Software: Update software regularly by employing patch management for internal enterprise endpoints and servers.
M1019 Threat Intelligence Program: Develop a robust cyber threat intelligence capability to determine what types and levels of threat may use software exploits and 0-days against a particular organization.
M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing: Make it difficult for adversaries to advance their operation through exploitation of undiscovered or unpatched vulnerabilities by using sandboxing. Other types of virtualization and application microsegmentation may also mitigate the impact of some types of exploitation. Risks of additional exploits and weaknesses in these systems may still exist.

name: Exploitation for Stealth
title: T1211 Exploitation for Stealth: threat groups that use it
text: Threat groups known to use T1211 Exploitation for Stealth (2): APT28, Velvet Ant.

name: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
title: T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: what it is
text:
T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution. Tactic: Stealth, Execution. Platforms: Windows.
Adversaries may take advantage of trusted developer utilities to proxy execution of malicious payloads. There are many utilities used for software development related tasks that can be used to execute code in various forms to assist in development, debugging, and reverse engineering. These utilities may often be signed with legitimate certificates that allow them to execute on a system and proxy execution of malicious code through a trusted process that effectively bypasses application control solutions.
Smart App Control is a feature of Windows that blocks applications it considers potentially malicious from running by verifying unsigned applications against a known safe list from a Microsoft cloud service before executing them. However, adversaries may leverage "reputation hijacking" to abuse an operating system’s trust of safe, signed applications that support the execution of arbitrary code. By leveraging Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution to run their malicious code, adversaries may bypass Smart App Control protections.

name: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
title: T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution.
Detection strategy: Behavior-chain, platform-aware detection strategy for T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (Windows).
Windows: A trusted/signed developer utility (parent) is executed in a non-developer context and (a) spawns suspicious children (e.g., powershell.exe, cmd.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, wscript.exe), (b) loads unsigned/user-writable DLLs, (c) writes and then runs a new PE from user-writable paths, and/or (d) immediately makes outbound network connections. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security, WinEventLog:Sysmon, WinEventLog:AppLocker.

name: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
title: T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1127 Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution.
M1038 Execution Prevention: Certain developer utilities should be blocked or restricted if not required.
M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content: Consider disabling software installation or execution from the internet via developer utilities.
M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program: Specific developer utilities may not be necessary within a given environment and should be removed if not used.

name: System Shutdown/Reboot
title: T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: what it is
text:
T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot. Tactic: Impact. Platforms: ESXi, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Windows.
Adversaries may shutdown/reboot systems to interrupt access to, or aid in the destruction of, those systems. Operating systems may contain commands to initiate a shutdown/reboot of a machine or network device. In some cases, these commands may also be used to initiate a shutdown/reboot of a remote computer or network device via Network Device CLI (e.g. reload). They may also include shutdown/reboot of a virtual machine via hypervisor / cloud consoles or command line tools.
Shutting down or rebooting systems may disrupt access to computer resources for legitimate users while also impeding incident response/recovery.
Adversaries may also use Windows API functions, such as `InitializeSystemShutdownExW` or `ExitWindowsEx`, to force a system to shut down or reboot. Alternatively, the `NtRaiseHardError`or `ZwRaiseHardError` Windows API functions with the `ResponseOption` parameter set to `OptionShutdownSystem` may deliver a “blue screen of death” (BSOD) to a system. In order to leverage these API functions, an adversary may need to acquire `SeShutdownPrivilege` (e.g., via Access Token Manipulation).
In some cases, the system may not be able to boot again.
Adversaries may attempt to shutdown/reboot a system after impacting it in other ways, such as Disk Structure Wipe or Inhibit System Recovery, to hasten the intended effects on system availability.

name: System Shutdown/Reboot
title: T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot.
Detection strategy: Multi-Platform Shutdown or Reboot Detection via Execution and Host Status Events.
Windows: Correlate process execution of shutdown/reboot commands (e.g., shutdown.exe, restart-computer) with host status change logs (Event IDs 1074, 6006) and absence of related administrative context (e.g., user not in Helpdesk group). Log sources: WinEventLog:Security, WinEventLog:Sysmon.
Linux: Detect 'shutdown', 'reboot', or 'systemctl poweroff' executions with auditd/syslog and absence of scheduled maintenance windows or approved user context. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL, linux:syslog.
macOS: Identify use of 'shutdown', 'reboot', or 'osascript' system shutdown invocations within unified logs and track unexpected shutdown sequences initiated by GUI or script. Cross-reference with user activity or absence thereof. Log sources: macos:unifiedlog.
ESXi: Detect commands such as 'esxcli system shutdown' or 'vim-cmd vmsvc/power.shutdown' executed outside of maintenance windows or via unusual users. Reboot logs in hostd.log and shell logs should be correlated. Log sources: esxi:hostd, esxi:shell.
Network Devices: Monitor CLI 'reload' commands issued without scheduled maintenance, and correlate to TACACS+/AAA logs for privilege validation. Log sources: networkdevice:syslog.

name: System Shutdown/Reboot
title: T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: threat groups that use it
text: Threat groups known to use T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot (4): APT37, APT38, Lazarus Group, Medusa Group.

name: MMC
title: T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC: what it is
text:
T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: Windows. It is a sub-technique of T1218 System Binary Proxy Execution.
Adversaries may abuse mmc.exe to proxy execution of malicious .msc files. Microsoft Management Console (MMC) is a binary that may be signed by Microsoft and is used in several ways in either its GUI or in a command prompt. MMC can be used to create, open, and save custom consoles that contain administrative tools created by Microsoft, called snap-ins. These snap-ins may be used to manage Windows systems locally or remotely. MMC can also be used to open Microsoft created .msc files to manage system configuration.
For example, mmc C:\Users\foo\admintools.msc /a will open a custom, saved console msc file in author mode. Another common example is mmc gpedit.msc, which will open the Group Policy Editor application window.
Adversaries may use MMC commands to perform malicious tasks. For example, mmc wbadmin.msc delete catalog -quiet deletes the backup catalog on the system (i.e. Inhibit System Recovery) without prompts to the user (Note: wbadmin.msc may only be present by default on Windows Server operating systems).

name: MMC
title: T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC: what it is
text:
T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: Windows. It is a sub-technique of T1218 System Binary Proxy Execution.
Adversaries may also abuse MMC to execute malicious .msc files. For example, adversaries may first create a malicious registry Class Identifier (CLSID) subkey, which uniquely identifies a Component Object Model class object. Then, adversaries may create custom consoles with the “Link to Web Address” snap-in that is linked to the malicious CLSID subkey. Once the .msc file is saved, adversaries may invoke the malicious CLSID payload with the following command: mmc.exe -Embedding C:\path\to\test.msc.

name: MMC
title: T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC.
Detection strategy: Detecting MMC (.msc) Proxy Execution and Malicious COM Activation.
Windows: Abuse of mmc.exe to execute non-Microsoft or user-staged .msc files and malicious COM CLSIDs. Behavioral chain: (1) suspicious mmc.exe invocation with /a or -Embedding and non-standard .msc path → (2) COM activation of non-baseline CLSIDs by mmc.exe → (3) mmc.exe loads non-baseline DLLs (user-writable/UNC/unsigned) → (4) optional network/DNS activity from mmc.exe. Log sources: WinEventLog:Sysmon, WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-COM/Operational, WinEventLog:PowerShell.

name: MMC
title: T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC.
M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program: MMC may not be necessary within a given environment since it is primarily used by system administrators, not regular users or clients.
M1038 Execution Prevention: Use application control configured to block execution of MMC if it is not required for a given system or network to prevent potential misuse by adversaries.

name: MMC
title: T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC: threat groups that use it
text: Threat groups known to use T1218.014 System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC (1): Medusa Group.

name: Process Argument Spoofing
title: T1564.010 Hide Artifacts: Process Argument Spoofing: what it is
text:
T1564.010 Hide Artifacts: Process Argument Spoofing. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: Windows. It is a sub-technique of T1564 Hide Artifacts.
Adversaries may attempt to hide process command-line arguments by overwriting process memory. Process command-line arguments are stored in the process environment block (PEB), a data structure used by Windows to store various information about/used by a process. The PEB includes the process command-line arguments that are referenced when executing the process. When a process is created, defensive tools/sensors that monitor process creations may retrieve the process arguments from the PEB.
Adversaries may manipulate a process PEB to evade defenses. For example, Process Hollowing can be abused to spawn a process in a suspended state with benign arguments. After the process is spawned and the PEB is initialized (and process information is potentially logged by tools/sensors), adversaries may override the PEB to modify the command-line arguments (ex: using the Native API WriteProcessMemory() function) then resume process execution with malicious arguments.
Adversaries may also execute a process with malicious command-line arguments then patch the memory with benign arguments that may bypass subsequent process memory analysis.
This behavior may also be combined with other tricks (such as Parent PID Spoofing) to manipulate or further evade process-based detections.

name: Process Argument Spoofing
title: T1564.010 Hide Artifacts: Process Argument Spoofing: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1564.010 Hide Artifacts: Process Argument Spoofing.
Detection strategy: Detection Strategy for Process Argument Spoofing on Windows.
Windows: Inconsistencies between process command-line arguments logged at creation time and subsequent process behavior. Defender perspective: monitoring for processes launched in a suspended state, followed by memory modifications (e.g., WriteProcessMemory targeting the PEB) that overwrite arguments before execution resumes. Detection also includes observing anomalous behaviors from processes whose logged arguments do not align with executed activity (e.g., network connections, file writes, or registry modifications). Log sources: WinEventLog:Security, WinEventLog:Sysmon.

name: COR_PROFILER
title: T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER: what it is
text:
T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER. Tactic: Stealth, Execution. Platforms: Windows. It is a sub-technique of T1574 Hijack Execution Flow.
Adversaries may leverage the COR_PROFILER environment variable to hijack the execution flow of programs that load the .NET CLR. The COR_PROFILER is a .NET Framework feature which allows developers to specify an unmanaged (or external of .NET) profiling DLL to be loaded into each .NET process that loads the Common Language Runtime (CLR). These profilers are designed to monitor, troubleshoot, and debug managed code executed by the .NET CLR.
The COR_PROFILER environment variable can be set at various scopes (system, user, or process) resulting in different levels of influence. System and user-wide environment variable scopes are specified in the Registry, where a Component Object Model (COM) object can be registered as a profiler DLL. A process scope COR_PROFILER can also be created in-memory without modifying the Registry. Starting with .NET Framework 4, the profiling DLL does not need to be registered as long as the location of the DLL is specified in the COR_PROFILER_PATH environment variable.
Adversaries may abuse COR_PROFILER to establish persistence that executes a malicious DLL in the context of all .NET processes every time the CLR is invoked. The COR_PROFILER can also be used to elevate privileges (ex: Bypass User Account Control) if the victim .NET process executes at a higher permission level, as well as to hook and impair defenses provided by .NET processes.

name: COR_PROFILER
title: T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER.
Detection strategy: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow using the Windows COR_PROFILER..
Windows: Modification of COR_PROFILER-related environment variables or Registry keys (COR_ENABLE_PROFILING, COR_PROFILER, COR_PROFILER_PATH), combined with anomalous .NET process creation or unmanaged DLL loads. Defender observes registry modifications, suspicious process creation with altered environment variables, and profiler DLLs loaded unexpectedly into .NET CLR processes. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security, WinEventLog:Sysmon.

name: COR_PROFILER
title: T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER.
M1024 Restrict Registry Permissions: Ensure proper permissions are set for Registry hives to prevent users from modifying keys associated with COR_PROFILER.
M1038 Execution Prevention: Identify and block potentially malicious unmanaged COR_PROFILER profiling DLLs by using application control solutions like AppLocker that are capable of auditing and/or blocking unapproved DLLs.
M1018 User Account Management: Limit the privileges of user accounts so that only authorized administrators can edit system environment variables.

name: COR_PROFILER
title: T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER: threat groups that use it
text: Threat groups known to use T1574.012 Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER (1): Blue Mockingbird.

name: Anti-Automation Evasion
title: T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion: what it is
text:
T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: SaaS.
Adversaries may employ various means to evade or complete automation checks. Automation checks distinguish human users from bot traffic and prevent bots from reaching the web pages protected by automation checks. For example, a user may be required to solve a CAPTCHA challenge before accessing a form or login page. Traditional CAPTCHAs ask the user to decipher a string of characters, type the characters into a box, and submit the form. reCAPTCHA asks the user to identify images, click a checkbox, or evaluate the user’s behavior from mouse movement and device cookies.
Adversaries may pay for a service that forwards the CAPTCHA challenge to a remote human worker. The human service then solves the CAPTCHA on behalf of the bot. AI tools, such as CapSolver, can also be used to automatically solve CAPTCHA challenges.

name: Anti-Automation Evasion
title: T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion.
Detection strategy: Detection of Anti-Automation Evasion.
SaaS: No target-side behavioral Detection Strategy exists for CAPTCHA based solely on CAPTCHA telemetry.

name: Anti-Automation Evasion
title: T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion.
M1037 Filter Network Traffic: Use web application firewalls, bot-management controls, and application-layer traffic filtering to restrict automated access to protected resources. Apply filtering using request characteristics, client/session reputation, behavioral signals, rate limits, and validated client or bot identity. Block, rate-limit, or challenge traffic that violates established access policies.
M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention: Deploy inline application-layer protections capable of identifying and preventing automated activity before requests reach protected application functionality. Use multiple automation signals rather than relying exclusively on successful CAPTCHA completion.

name: Steal Application Specific Passwords
title: T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords: what it is
text:
T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords. Tactic: Credential Access. Platforms: Office Suite, Identity Provider, SaaS.
Adversaries may steal Application Specific Passwords (ASPs) to gain access to Valid Accounts, bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) methods. ASPs are passwords typically used to give third-party applications or legacy devices (which do not support MFA methods) account access.
An adversary may socially engineer a user into providing an ASP (using methods like Phishing for Information), generate an ASP for an already compromised account, or obtain an ASP stored on a system. Afterward, adversaries may use the ASP to access Valid Accounts and, in some cases, maintain Persistence, bypassing any form of MFA set on the account.

name: Steal Application Specific Passwords
title: T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords.
Detection strategy: Suspicious Acquisition and Use of Application-Specific Passwords.
SaaS: Detect successful SaaS authentication through an application-specific or legacy credential mechanism from a source/client not previously associated with that account, correlated with new session establishment or subsequent access inconsistent with ApprovedASPUsage. Log sources: saas:audit , saas:audit, saas:session .
Office Suite: Detect successful Office Suite access using an authentication method that does not perform the account's expected MFA flow, correlated within ASPActivityWindow with first-seen client/application access, an anomalous source/device, or an ASP-related account credential change where available. Log sources: m365:unified, azure:signinlogs, idp:audit.
Identity Provider: Detect creation of an application-specific password for a user account, correlated within ASPActivityWindow with authentication from a source, device, client, or location outside the account's established baseline, or followed by authentication using a legacy/non-MFA authentication path inconsistent with ApprovedASPUsage. Log sources: idp:audit, idp:authentication , idp:session .

name: Steal Application Specific Passwords
title: T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords.
M1017 User Training: ASPs can be obtained through social engineering, which your technique explicitly includes. Train users not to generate or disclose ASPs in response to unsolicited instructions.
M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program: Disable ASP functionality where modern authentication is available. Microsoft specifically supports disabling users' ability to create app passwords and recommends disabling legacy authentication so existing app passwords no longer work.
M1036 Account Use Policies: Restrict authentication paths/clients/locations through which accounts using legacy/app-password authentication can authenticate. This matters because an ASP that has been stolen shouldn't automatically have unrestricted account reach.
M1018 User Account Management: Restrict which users may create/use ASPs; disable ASP creation where unnecessary; remove existing ASPs. Microsoft allows admins to disable creation and separately delete existing ASPs; Google administrators can view/revoke users' application-specific passwords.

name: Steal Application Specific Passwords
title: T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords: threat groups that use it
text: Threat groups known to use T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords (1): APT42.

name: Indirect Prompt Injection
title: T1698 Indirect Prompt Injection: what it is
text:
T1698 Indirect Prompt Injection. Tactic: Execution. Platforms: Windows, SaaS.
Adversaries may deliver malicious prompts to an LLM indirectly by embedding the prompts in content that the adversary expects may be processed by an LLM. These prompts can be included in web pages, documents, emails, tickets, code, or other sources that an agent, copilot, or other AI system may retrieve and process. When an LLM processes this content, the embedded instructions may cause the system to perform unintended behaviors.
Adversaries may use indirect prompt injection to Impair Autonomous Defenses, and for unauthorized execution of any capabilities available to the LLM.

name: Indirect Prompt Injection
title: T1698 Indirect Prompt Injection: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1698 Indirect Prompt Injection.
M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Restrict AI agents to files, directories, repositories, and content stores required for their approved workflows. Limit write access separately from read access where possible to reduce the actions available following successful indirect prompt injection.
M1026 Privileged Account Management: Prevent AI agents processing untrusted or externally controlled content from automatically exercising privileged permissions. Require additional authorization for sensitive operations derived from retrieved content.
M1038 Execution Prevention: Prevent instructions contained in retrieved or externally supplied content from independently authorizing consequential agent actions. Require tool/API requests derived from external content to satisfy authorization and policy controls independent of the model-generated decision.
M1030 Network Segmentation: Restrict network resources and external destinations accessible to AI agents that process untrusted content. Limit outbound communication and access to unrelated internal services to reduce exfiltration and lateral effects following successful injection.
M1018 User Account Management: Use dedicated identities for AI agents and restrict their permissions to the minimum resources and actions required by the approved workflow. Do not allow retrieved content to change the authorization context associated with the agent.
M1017 User Training: Train users and administrators to treat content processed by AI agents as potentially adversarial and to require independent validation before approving sensitive actions proposed as a result of externally sourced content.

name: Direct Prompt Injection
title: T1699 Direct Prompt Injection: what it is
text:
T1699 Direct Prompt Injection. Tactic: Execution. Platforms: Windows, SaaS.
Adversaries may input malicious prompts directly into an LLM’s user interface. The prompts can be designed to bypass safeguards, manipulate context, override previous instructions, or coerce the LLM into unauthorized behavior.
Adversaries may use direct prompt injection to Generate Content prohibited by the LLM's guardrails or to induce the system to utilize its capabilities in unintended or prohibited ways. Adversaries may achieve this by instructing the LLM to ignore previous instructions or safety rules, or by impersonating a role such as a researcher or privileged user.

name: Direct Prompt Injection
title: T1699 Direct Prompt Injection: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1699 Direct Prompt Injection.
M1018 User Account Management: Associate AI interactions with authenticated identities and constrain AI-mediated actions to the permissions of the initiating user. Do not allow prompt content to establish or elevate the authorization context used by downstream tools or services.
M1038 Execution Prevention: Prevent user-supplied AI prompts from directly authorizing consequential actions. Enforce tool, API, command, and resource authorization outside the model and reject requested actions that exceed the permissions associated with the initiating user or agent task.
M1017 User Training: Train users responsible for AI-enabled systems to recognize attempts to manipulate system instructions, role boundaries, or safety controls through user-provided prompts and to independently validate consequential AI-generated actions.
M1026 Privileged Account Management: Restrict access to privileged AI capabilities and require explicit authorization or human approval for AI-generated actions involving administrative functions, sensitive resources, or privileged tools.

name: AI Result Poisoning
title: T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning: what it is
text:
T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning. Tactic: Resource Development. Platforms: PRE. It is a sub-technique of T1608 Stage Capabilities.
Adversaries may manipulate publicly accessible web content to influence generative AI systems or AI-powered search engines into retrieving, citing, or recommending attacker-controlled information.
Unlike traditional SEO Poisoning, which primarily attempts to influence the ordering of conventional search results, AI Result Poisoning targets systems that synthesize information from multiple sources and provide a direct answer to the user. Adversaries may create malicious or misleading websites, publish fabricated claims, generate supporting articles, or establish multiple apparently independent sources that reinforce the same information. These sources may then be retrieved by AI systems using web search or retrieval-augmented generation and incorporated into generated responses.
Adversaries may use this technique to recommend or link to phishing sites, fraudulent online stores, malicious downloads, impersonation pages, or other attacker-controlled infrastructure. It can also be used to promote misinformation or fabricated claims without requiring access to the underlying AI model, system prompt, or application infrastructure. Because the malicious content can resemble ordinary marketing, editorial, or informational material, traditional prompt injection and malware-focused detections may not identify the activity.

name: AI Result Poisoning
title: T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning.
Detection strategy: Detection of AI Result Poisoning.
PRE: No target-side behavioral analytic. A defender cannot reliably distinguish an adversary intentionally staging public content to manipulate future AI retrieval from ordinary publishing, SEO, inaccurate information, duplicated content, or legitimate coordinated publication using target-enterprise telemetry.

name: AI Result Poisoning
title: T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning.
M1056 Pre-compromise: This technique cannot be easily mitigated with preventive controls since it is based on behaviors performed outside of the scope of enterprise defenses and controls.

name: Automate CAPTCHA Completion
title: T1696.001 Anti-Automation Evasion: Automate CAPTCHA Completion: what it is
text:
T1696.001 Anti-Automation Evasion: Automate CAPTCHA Completion. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: SaaS. It is a sub-technique of T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion.
Adversaries may attempt to use bots to successfully solve CAPTCHA challenges. CAPTCHA challenges are typically used by defenders to detect and prevent bot and spam traffic from accessing protected webpages. CAPTCHAs are automated tests often placed before login screens or form fields. Traditional CAPTCHAs ask the user to decipher a string of characters, type the characters into a box, and submit the form. reCAPTCHA asks the user to identify images, click a checkbox, or evaluate the user’s behavior from mouse movement and device cookies.
Adversaries may use scripts or toolkits to automatically solve the CAPTCHA puzzle. For example, adversaries may develop a script that uses the ImageMagick toolkit to solve the CAPTCHA puzzles to then create multiple valid accounts. ImageMagick tool can convert the images into a RGB complemented image. The CAPTCHA challenge may be solved by identifying and comparing attributes of the RGB images to select the expected image. Once the CAPTCHA challenge is solved, the adversary’s script may access the protected page. After accessing the protected the page, the adversary may submit valid forms to the target.

name: Automate CAPTCHA Completion
title: T1696.001 Anti-Automation Evasion: Automate CAPTCHA Completion: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1696.001 Anti-Automation Evasion: Automate CAPTCHA Completion.
Detection strategy: Detection of Automated CAPTCHA.
SaaS: Successful CAPTCHA completion does not expose whether the challenge was solved manually, through automated tooling, through an AI-enabled solver, or through a third-party human-solving service. Providers may independently classify associated sessions as automated or bot-like, but this identifies suspicious automation rather than the method used to complete the CAPTCHA.

name: Automate CAPTCHA Completion
title: T1696.001 Anti-Automation Evasion: Automate CAPTCHA Completion: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1696.001 Anti-Automation Evasion: Automate CAPTCHA Completion.
M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention: Configure inline bot-management and web application protections to continue enforcing automation controls after a client successfully completes a CAPTCHA. Use challenge-token state as one input rather than as a durable trust determination, and prevent requests that subsequently exhibit automated or abusive behavior.
M1037 Filter Network Traffic: Do not treat successful CAPTCHA completion alone as sufficient evidence that subsequent activity is human-generated. Continue evaluating requests using bot classification, request rate, client/session characteristics, token reuse, source reputation, and behavioral signals after successful challenge completion. Block or rate-limit activity that remains inconsistent with expected human use.

name: Avoid CAPTCHA
title: T1696.002 Anti-Automation Evasion: Avoid CAPTCHA: what it is
text:
T1696.002 Anti-Automation Evasion: Avoid CAPTCHA. Tactic: Stealth. Platforms: SaaS. It is a sub-technique of T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion.
Adversaries may avoid CAPTCHA challenges by mimicking human behavior. Automation tests, such as CAPTCHA, are typically used by defenders to detect and prevent bot and spam traffic from accessing protected webpages. CAPTCHAs are often placed before login screens or form fields. Traditional CAPTCHAs ask the user to decipher a string of characters, type the characters into a box, and submit the form. reCAPTCHA asks the user to identify images, click a checkbox, or evaluate the user’s behavior from mouse movement and device cookies.
Adversaries may attempt to avoid CAPTCHA challenges by constructing a bot that mimics human behavior through browser automation. The automated browser may mimic a human by Masquerading a Browser Fingerprint and through attributes such as session history, IP reputation, and the use of browser APIs. For example, adversaries may use Selenium browsers to simulate a human user. In the Selenium browsers, JavaScript is injected into the website’s Document Object Model (DOM). The injected script may modify browser attributes such as Audio Context and Voice engines, graphic rendering, installed fonts, and browser navigator objects.

name: Avoid CAPTCHA
title: T1696.002 Anti-Automation Evasion: Avoid CAPTCHA: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1696.002 Anti-Automation Evasion: Avoid CAPTCHA.
Detection strategy: Detection of Avoid CAPTCHA.
SaaS: No target-side behavioral Detection Strategy exists for Avoid CAPTCHA based solely on CAPTCHA telemetry.

name: Avoid CAPTCHA
title: T1696.002 Anti-Automation Evasion: Avoid CAPTCHA: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1696.002 Anti-Automation Evasion: Avoid CAPTCHA.
M1037 Filter Network Traffic: Apply bot-management and application-layer filtering independently of whether a CAPTCHA challenge is triggered. Evaluate protected requests using behavioral, client/session, rate, reputation, token, and automation signals, and block or rate-limit activity that violates policy even when no CAPTCHA was presented.
M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention: Deploy layered inline controls that prevent automated access based on observed request and session behavior rather than relying solely on challenge presentation. Use silent challenges, browser/client validation, rate controls, and bot-management signals to prevent clients that mimic legitimate users from obtaining unrestricted access to protected functionality.

name: Impair Autonomous Defenses
title: T1685.007 Disable or Modify Tools: Impair Autonomous Defenses: what it is
text:
T1685.007 Disable or Modify Tools: Impair Autonomous Defenses. Tactic: Defense Impairment. Platforms: Windows, SaaS. It is a sub-technique of T1685 Disable or Modify Tools.
Adversaries may use methods like Indirect Prompt Injection to disrupt, disable, or otherwise impair autonomous defensive capabilities such as LLM-assisted processing of malware, artifacts, or activity. This behavior may cause a system to ignore data, fail to alert on malicious activity, abort analysis, or to be disabled completely.
Adversaries may include content in malware implants that mimic an LLM prompt scaffold that contains fake system messages in order to convince the LLM that it has encountered an error. Depending on the type of error, the LLM may abort analysis, truncate, or refuse to continue. Adversaries may also embed prompts in malware intended to stop agents or systems from analyzing the malware.

name: Impair Autonomous Defenses
title: T1685.007 Disable or Modify Tools: Impair Autonomous Defenses: how to prevent it
text:
Mitigations for T1685.007 Disable or Modify Tools: Impair Autonomous Defenses.
M1038 Execution Prevention: Prevent content contained within an artifact under analysis from directly controlling the analysis workflow, terminating analysis, altering required analysis stages, or initiating unrelated tools and actions. Enforce workflow transitions independently of instructions generated from artifact content.
M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Limit AI-assisted analysis systems to the files and directories required for analysis and prevent artifacts under investigation from modifying agent configuration, instruction files, analysis state, or other trusted AI application resources.
M1047 Audit: Require AI-assisted security analysis workflows to preserve analysis status, artifact provenance, tool execution, termination reason, and completion state so that incomplete or unexpectedly redirected analysis can be independently identified and reviewed.
M1026 Privileged Account Management: Prevent AI-assisted analysis agents from exercising privileged capabilities solely as a consequence of artifact-derived instructions. Require independent authorization for privileged or consequential operations outside the expected analysis workflow.
M1018 User Account Management: Run AI-assisted analysis services using dedicated identities with permissions limited to required analysis functions. Separate analysis authority from broader analyst, administrative, or production access.

name: AI-Enabled Exfiltration
title: T1700 AI-Enabled Exfiltration: what it is
text:
T1700 AI-Enabled Exfiltration. Tactic: Exfiltration. Platforms: Windows, SaaS.
Adversaries may utilize Direct Prompt Injection, Indirect Prompt Injection or other methods to instruct enterprise AI agents to exfiltrate data. When enterprise systems incorporate the use of AI assistants or other AI agents, adversaries may abuse these systems to weaponize sanctioned tools available to the agent.
As an AI agent processes queries or ingests data, an injected prompt can cause the agent to use its tool connections in unauthorized or unintended ways. When AI agents are induced to exfiltrate data, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as Exfiltration to Code Repository or Exfiltration Over Web Service.

name: AI-Enabled Exfiltration
title: T1700 AI-Enabled Exfiltration: how to detect it
text:
How to detect T1700 AI-Enabled Exfiltration.
Detection strategy: Detect AI-Enabled Exfiltration.
Windows: An analyst observes an AI-associated process access data outside $AuthorizedAIDataScope$, followed within $EndpointExfilWindow$ by transfer-capable execution and an outbound connection to a destination outside $AuthorizedAIEndpoints$ from the same process lineage. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security, WinEventLog:PowerShell, WinEventLog:Sysmon.

name: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
title: CVE-2026-20127: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
text:
CVE-2026-20127: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager Authentication Bypass Vulnerability. Vendor: Cisco. Product: Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager. This vulnerability is in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue: it has been exploited in the wild. Added to KEV: 2026-02-25. Known use in ransomware campaigns: Unknown.
Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, formerly SD-WAN vSmart, and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, formerly SD-WAN vManage, contain an authentication bypass vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to bypass authentication and obtain administrative privileges on an affected system. This vulnerability exists because the peering authentication mechanism in an affected system is not working properly. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted requests to an affected system. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to log in to an affected Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller as an internal, high-privileged, non-root user account. Using this account, the attacker could access NETCONF, which would then allow the attacker to manipulate network configuration for the SD-WAN fabric.
Required action: Please adhere to CISA’s guidelines to assess exposure and mitigate risks associated with Cisco SD-WAN devices as outlines in CISA’s Emergency Directive 26-03 (URL listed below in Notes) and CISA’s “Hunt & Hardening Guidance for Cisco SD-WAN Devices (URL listed below in Notes). title: CVE-2025-27915: Synacor Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) Cross-site Scripting Vulnerability
text:

Synacor Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability that exists in the Classic Web Client due to insufficient sanitization of HTML content in ICS files. When a user views an e-mail message containing a malicious ICS entry, its embedded JavaScript executes via an ontoggle event inside a tag. This allows an attacker to run arbitrary JavaScript within the victim's session, potentially leading to unauthorized actions such as setting e-mail filters to redirect messages to an attacker-controlled address. As a result, an attacker can perform unauthorized actions on the victim's account, including e-mail redirection and data exfiltration.

name: Cisco IOS XE Web UI Command Injection Vulnerability
title: CVE-2023-20273: Cisco IOS XE Web UI Command Injection Vulnerability
text:
CVE-2023-20273: Cisco IOS XE Web UI Command Injection Vulnerability. Vendor: Cisco. Product: Cisco IOS XE Web UI. This vulnerability is in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue: it has been exploited in the wild. Added to KEV: 2023-10-23. Known use in ransomware campaigns: Unknown.
Cisco IOS XE contains a command injection vulnerability in the web user interface. When chained with CVE-2023-20198, the attacker can leverage the new local user to elevate privilege to root and write the implant to the file system. Cisco identified CVE-2023-20273 as the vulnerability exploited to deploy the implant. CVE-2021-1435, previously associated with the exploitation events, is no longer believed to be related to this activity.
Required action: Verify that instances of Cisco IOS XE Web UI are in compliance with BOD 23-02 and apply mitigations per vendor instructions. For affected products (Cisco IOS XE Web UI exposed to the internet or to untrusted networks), follow vendor instructions to determine if a system may have been compromised and immediately report positive findings to CISA. Due date for US federal agencies: 2023-10-27.
